t018: An alternative to Polar Beat and other popular apps.
t019: Live heart rate. Useful workout data.

t024: See your BPM, current zone, live heart rate chart and time in each zone. Audio and vibration alerts help you keep track of your effort without checking the screen.
t026: Record your GPS route, pace, speed, duration and distance while running, cycling or hiking.
t027: Track heart rate with your screen off
t028: Your workout continues recording in the background. Heart rate, pace and distance remain available in the system notification on your lock screen.
t030: Workout count, distance, total duration, average heart rate and time in each zone help you see how your training adds up.
t033: Enter your date of birth, set your maximum heart rate and choose the standard or Karvonen method. The five zone boundaries are calculated from your data.

t036: Review distance, duration, average and maximum heart rate after your workout. The route, chart and time in each zone show how your effort changed throughout the session.
t040: Connect your heart rate strap, monitor your workout and share your progress. Here is what PulseZones can do on Android.
t041: Which Bluetooth chest straps work with PulseZones?
t042: Connect a compatible Bluetooth Low Energy sensor directly in PulseZones. The developer has personally tested the GEOID HS500, Magene H303 and Magene H603. Other models need to support the standard Bluetooth Heart Rate Service.
t043: Can I see live heart rate from my chest strap on Android?
t044: Follow your current heart rate, zone number and chart during your session. The home screen also shows the connected sensor and its battery status.
t045: How can I track time in heart rate zones?
t046: Five color-coded zones show your workout intensity. Follow your current zone and the time spent in each zone as your workout progresses.
t047: Does the app have heart rate zone alerts?
t048: Yes. Choose a target zone and get an alert when you leave it, or enable alerts whenever you move between zones. Sound and vibration let you follow your effort without looking at your phone.
t049: Can I use Karvonen heart rate reserve zones?
t050: Choose the Karvonen method and enter your resting heart rate. The standard method uses percentages of maximum heart rate. Set your maximum manually or use an age-based estimate.
t052: Can I track GPS routes, running pace and cycling speed?
t053: Enable GPS recording to track your route, distance, duration, speed and pace. Choose kilometers or miles and switch between the map and heart rate chart during your workout.
t054: Does heart rate recording work in the background?
t055: PulseZones keeps recording an active workout in the background. Heart rate, pace and distance are available in the system notification, including on the lock screen.
t056: Where can I see my workout history and heart rate charts?
t057: Open a saved session in your history to see duration, distance, average and maximum heart rate, the chart, time in zones and your recorded route in one report.
t058: How do I share my workout results?
t059: Open a saved workout and use Share to send the report to your coach, friends or training group.
t060: Can I see weekly and monthly training statistics?
t061: Choose a period and activity type to see your workout count, total distance and duration, average heart rate, daily distance and time in each heart rate zone.
t062: How do I share weekly or monthly training statistics?
t063: Select a week or month in Statistics and share the summary report. It is a convenient way to show your training volume and intensity distribution for the whole period.
t064: Which app supports running, cycling and strength training?
t065: PulseZones includes running, cycling, hiking, strength, cardio, sport and sleep modes, plus a demo mode. Choose a mode for your session and review statistics by activity type.
t066: Is PulseZones a free heart rate monitor app with no ads?
t067: Yes. There are no ads, subscriptions or mandatory sign-ups. You need a compatible Bluetooth heart rate sensor: PulseZones reads the sensor's data rather than measuring your pulse with the phone camera.
t068: Can I record heart rate and workouts offline?
t069: Core PulseZones features work offline. Your profile, workout history and routes are stored locally on your smartphone.
t070: Which languages does the heart rate monitor app support?
t071: PulseZones supports ten languages: English, Russian, Spanish, Brazilian Portuguese, German, French, Italian, Polish, Turkish and Georgian.
t072: How can I make heart rate readings easier to read?
t073: Adjust the text size in the app to make workout metrics easier to read.
t074: Where does the app get its heart rate data?
t075: PulseZones displays readings transmitted by the connected sensor. It does not invent heart rate values or replace them with calculated estimates. Measurement accuracy depends on the sensor, skin contact and connection quality.
t076: How does the app process GPS routes?
t077: Coordinates come from your phone's location system. PulseZones smooths suspicious jumps and processes the track before saving to reduce the effects of GPS errors. Processing cannot replace a good signal: route quality still depends on your phone and reception conditions.
t078: Looking for another app for your heart rate strap?

t082: The core tasks are similar: monitor heart rate, record a workout and GPS route, and review the results afterwards. PulseZones focuses on intensity settings, accessible metrics and convenient reports.
t084: Choose the standard or Karvonen calculation, set your maximum heart rate and enter your resting heart rate for Karvonen. This lets you choose how the boundaries of your five zones are calculated.
t087: Set an alert for leaving a specific zone when you want to maintain a target effort. Alternatively, enable alerts for transitions between all zones to follow intensity changes throughout your workout.
t089: Your sensor's connection and battery status appear on the home screen. As soon as you connect, you can check its current status and get ready to train.
t090: Metrics stay visible above the map and chart
t091: Switch between the heart rate chart and map during an active workout: the top metrics panel stays in place. Both views show heart rate, distance, duration and pace or speed.
t093: Alongside individual workout reports, PulseZones provides weekly and monthly statistics. Choose a period and activity type, review training volume and time in zones, then share the summary with your coach or friends.
t095: Choose English, Russian, Spanish, Brazilian Portuguese, German, French, Italian, Polish, Turkish or Georgian to view your metrics in a familiar language.
t097: You do not need an account to use PulseZones. The app is free, with no ads or subscription. Workout history and routes are stored on your phone.

t114: Connect your Bluetooth heart rate monitor to Android
t115: PulseZones works with BLE sensors that transmit heart rate using the standard Bluetooth Heart Rate Service.
t116: Put on and activate your sensor
t117: Moisten the strap electrodes and secure the strap around your chest. Most sensors turn on automatically.
t119: Allow Bluetooth and nearby device access, then select your sensor in the app.
t121: Choose an activity and tap Start. After your session, disconnect the sensor and remember to take it off. We also recommend detaching the sensor from the strap.
t123: GEOID HS500, Magene H303 and Magene H603. Other models may also work if they support the standard BLE Heart Rate Service.
t127: Check Permissions and background operation in PulseZones settings. It helps you prepare your phone for stable operation during workouts, including with the screen off.
t128: Nearby devices: connect your Bluetooth sensor
t129: Allow nearby device discovery and connection so PulseZones can find your heart rate monitor and receive its data. Bluetooth must also be enabled on your phone. The permission name and whether a separate prompt appears depend on your Android version.
t131: Allow precise location while using the app and turn on your phone's location services to record GPS routes, distance, speed and pace. The app requests this permission when you enable route recording. Heart rate recording still works without it.
t132: Notifications: view your workout in the background
t133: Allow PulseZones notifications to see your current heart rate, available pace or speed during GPS recording, and sensor connection status when the app is minimised or your screen is off.
t134: Unrestricted battery use: keep long workouts recording
t135: Allow PulseZones to run without battery restrictions. Power-saving settings may limit background operation, disconnect the sensor or stop recording. Find PulseZones in your battery settings and choose Unrestricted, Don't optimise or the equivalent option.
t136: Lock screen: check metrics without unlocking
t137: Allow PulseZones notifications on the lock screen. If Live heart rate, Sensor connection and Workout route are separate categories, check each one. Whether notification contents are visible also depends on your lock-screen privacy settings.
t138: Autostart: if your phone offers this setting
t139: Some manufacturers apply additional limits to app startup and background operation. If your system has an autostart setting, allow it for PulseZones. Not having this option does not, by itself, mean anything is wrong.
t140: Why does PulseZones still show a battery optimization warning?
t141: On some phones, allowing background operation and exempting an app from battery optimisation are separate settings. PulseZones checks whether Android confirms the optimisation exemption. The warning may therefore remain even after background operation is allowed.
t142: Find Battery optimisation in system settings, choose All apps if necessary, then select PulseZones. Check what the switch actually controls: Don't allow may refer to disallowing battery optimisation, rather than preventing the app from running.
t144: Names, menu paths and available switches depend on the manufacturer, model, Android version and system interface. Check the manufacturer's manual or support pages. If you cannot find an option, search online using your exact model, for example: '[model] allow app background activity', '[model] disable battery optimisation for app' or '[model] lock screen notifications'. Include your system version, because menus can change after an update.
t145: How do I check that recording continues with the screen off?
t146: Connect your sensor, start a short workout and turn the screen off for a few minutes. Then check that heart rate recording and, if GPS is enabled, route recording continued. A trial session helps reveal restrictions on your particular phone.
t147: Why train with heart rate zones?
t148: Heart rate zone training: match your effort to your goal
t149: Your heart rate gives you a sense of how hard you’re working. Heart rate zones group those readings into ranges, so you can tell an easy effort from a harder one at a glance.
t150: Use zones to keep an easy run easy, stay close to your target effort, or compare similar workouts. The boundaries are estimates, and they can change depending on how you calculate them.
t164: Pulse zones for easy runs and interval workouts
t165: You head out for an easy run. Then you push up a hill or pick up the pace to catch another runner. Before long, the run feels harder than you planned. A quick look at your heart rate zone can help you decide whether to ease off.
t166: Training pulse zones, also called heart rate zones, group heart rates into ranges based on effort. PulseZones shows five zones, from light effort to high intensity.
t167: Use heart rate to keep easy runs easy
t168: If the goal is to build mileage, keep the effort easy enough that you finish with some energy left for your next workout.
t169: The same pace can feel harder on a hill or on a hot day. If your heart rate climbs out of your target zone, try slowing down and see how your effort feels.
t170: Try the talk test too. At moderate intensity, you can usually talk but would struggle to sing.
t171: Follow effort and recovery during interval training
t172: During interval training, you alternate hard efforts with easier recovery. The heart rate chart shows how your pulse rose and fell. After the workout, time in each zone shows where you spent most of the session.
t173: Your heart rate can take time to catch up. On a short interval it may peak near the end, then stay high as you slow down. Use pace, interval length, and how the effort feels to guide the next rep.
t174: Look at the whole workout afterwards
t175: Two 40-minute runs can look very different. An easy run might stay mostly in one zone, while intervals may show a pattern of harder efforts and recovery.
t176: After the run, check your heart rate chart and time in each zone in PulseZones. Did the easy run stay easy? How did your pulse change between hard intervals and recovery?
t177: Read the zones alongside how you felt and what you set out to do that day.

t183: Heart rate zones: percentage of max HR vs Karvonen
t184: PulseZones can calculate heart rate zones in two ways. The standard method uses your maximum heart rate. The Karvonen method also uses your resting heart rate.
t186: Standard method: percentage of max heart rate
t187: In PulseZones, the five standard zones start at 50%, 60%, 70%, 80%, and 90% of your maximum heart rate.
t188: Zone boundary = maximum heart rate × percentage
t189: For example, with a maximum heart rate of
t193: To get started, use your known maximum heart rate or an approximate age-based estimate. PulseZones uses the formula
t195: Two people with the same maximum heart rate get the same zone boundaries with this method, even if their resting heart rates differ.
t198: Subtract your resting heart rate from your maximum to get your heart rate reserve. The Karvonen method takes a percentage of that reserve and adds it to your resting heart rate.
t199: Boundary = resting HR + (maximum HR − resting HR) × percentage
t201: and a resting heart rate of
t205: That puts the Karvonen boundary 24 bpm higher in this example. The two methods apply the same percentage to different numbers.
t206: Why does Karvonen use resting heart rate?
t207: Think of your heart rate reserve as the gap between your resting and maximum heart rates. At any given pulse, Karvonen shows how far you’ve moved through that gap.
t208: A different resting heart rate changes the size of the gap, even when two people have the same maximum.
t209: The same heart rate, a different share of the reserve
t210: Imagine two people with the same maximum heart rate of
t211: . The first has a resting heart rate of 50; the second, 80. Both reach 140 during exercise.
t212: Comparison at a heart rate of 140 bpm
t221: The standard method gives both people the same intensity: about 78% of maximum. Karvonen accounts for their different starting points:
t223: . This illustrates the calculation; it does not prove that one person necessarily feels a harder effort.
t224: Why is it more individual, but not always more accurate?
t225: Accounting for resting heart rate makes the calculation more personal. In exercise studies, the percentage of heart rate reserve generally tracks the percentage of oxygen uptake reserve more closely than the percentage of maximum heart rate does.
t226: Resting heart rate is influenced by fitness, individual characteristics and your current condition. A lower resting heart rate often accompanies improved endurance, but is not, on its own, a measure of health or fitness.
t228: The standard method is a simple starting point. If you know your usual resting heart rate, try Karvonen. A few calm morning readings before coffee or activity can give you a better sense of your usual resting pulse than one reading.
t229: Both methods depend on the numbers you enter. If you use 220 − age to estimate your maximum heart rate, your zone boundaries are estimates too.
t230: Following a training plan? Check how it defines its zones and compare the actual BPM ranges. Zone 2 in your plan may cover a different range from Zone 2 in an app.
